ing the stfeets. Before I left England last year I took occasion to visit Woolwich arsenal, and I saw the operations connected with the manufacture of guns and shells and fuses, and of all the articles that are needed in war. I spent syne time there, and took complete notes of every operation in that connection. I have a knowledge of machine tools, and of automatic machinery, so that I apprehend everything that was done in that arsenal. And let me say that I saw nothing done there which the people of this country could not do just as well. We have workmen just as able, and engineers that will hold their own with the engineers at Woolwich.
We must endeavour before this - war is over to put ourselves in a position to reap every advantage from Our great natural conditions. What a great thing it would be if this country were to become the greatest munition and arm producing country in the world. We have a monopoly of the raw materials that make cannon. To make cannon requires a certain amount of nickel, and also a certain amount of chrome, otherwise the temper of the metal will not last when the gun is fired quickly. We are spending enough money on this war to build these great plants for us and operate them. Now is our opportunity. If we let it pass it may never come again. If we deprive the Germans of our nickel, their predominance as an arm producing country will cease for ever. We will not be	troubled with so	many wars.
That is the whole secret of it. In all these localities we should be doing everything we can to bring about the establishment of works of this kind. I know that the Government have had a great many things to contend with and that they cannot do everything. I am speaking freely because, as a result of this great war, we have thrown our text books on economy into the fire and we have also thrown away a great deal of our politics.
1 think that some steps should be taken to inaugurate a policy similar to that carried out by Mr. Lloyd George in the old country. When he found that there were only three or four industries in Great Britain making shells and guns, and that they were trying to " hog " it all, he realized that it was necessary for him to get busy and increase the output of munitions. He called on the shoemakers, the cloth manufacturers and the steel makers and he said to these people: "We want you to make
material for the army." They said: "We have not any money to go into the manufacture of these articles." "Why?" he asked. They said: "We must have money with which to get machinery; the machinery that we require to make that stuff will be of no value after the war. Times are hard, we have no money, we have been fighting the Germans in the matter of commerce for years &nd we are without funds for the purchase of new machinery." That was true. He said: "You name what you want and the Government will provide you with it; if you want machinery for making munitions the Government will give you the capital that you require." He went to the manufacturers of clothing, of rifles, of shells, and made the same proposition to them. Hundreds of factories were established ia that way and to-day they are all going and prosperous. They are making large returns on their capital. Now, Mr. Lloyd George goes back to these manufacturers and says: "Well, gentlemen, you have made enough money to pay for these machines, for which the Government advanced you capital, you have got everything in first-class shape, you are making big profits and now I think the time has come when the Government should go into partnership with you and take 25 per cent of your earnings.." He is therefore quite justified in doing that. Something of that kind ought to be done in this country.
The day has gone by when we can stick fast to the old policy of letting everybody look after himself. England has advanced one hundred years in that respect during the last two years. Take it from me, if you had mentioned in England three years ago that there was a possibility of the Government taking over the railways of that country you would have been laughed at. you would have been told that there were so many interests at stake that nobody could get legislation of that kind through the British House of Commons. Yet, in one night the Government took over the railways of Great Britain and, with the exception of one or two small branches, they are bow all under Government operation and control. The Government have gone behind the munition manufacturers and they are going to go behind other kinds of manufacturers. Read the debates that are taking place in the English House of Commons almost every day and see what members of Parliament are saying about what they are going to do after the

war. They tell you that the Government are going to arrange banking 5 p.m. facilities, that they are going to stand behind their own manufacturers and that they are going to use every means in their power to control the commerce of the world. That is the proper policy and it is time that we should consider a policy of that kind.
I have talked to the House possibly long enough. There is nothing, as far as this war is concerned, that interests us more than the future. I see a glorious future arising from this war for this country and for the whole Empire. No longer will the British Empire be regarded as a bundle of sticks, a collection of shreds and patches. You will see, before this war is over, representatives of all the colonies having seats in the House of Commons; I have ne hesitation in saying that. But, there is plenty of time for that. The war is not going to be over to-morrow. We must not be in a hurry. We must do everything in our power to achieve the victory which we all hope for. If necessary, this House and this Government should take steps to assure the Mother Country that whatever can be done to bring about victory and the consolidation of the Empire we are prepared to do. Let us all pray that the day will come when we shall have, not an inglorious peace, but a splendid victory crowning our arms and sanctifying the sacrifices of our soldiers and people, when we shall have a great, free, united, happy and prosperous Empire presided over-as the great Pitt prayed for-by a pious and patriotic King and Emperor.

Mr. Speaker, as this is the first time I have spoken since you have occupied the Chair,
I would like to congratulate you on your rapid elevation, and to express the hope and belief that you will discharge the duties not only with honour to yourself but with credi.t to the high position which you occupy. I also desire to congratulate the Government on the choice of a Deputy Sp'eaker. The hon. gentleman who occupies that position (Mr. Rhodes) is a very strong personal friend of mine, and I think that both sides of the House will be satisfied with his discharge of the duties of the Deputy Speaker.
I would like to congratulate my hon. friend the-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) on the very lucid and brief manner in which he placed the Budget before the House. I also desire to congratulate the gallant colonel from North Sirocoe (Mr. 
John A. Currie) who has just taken his seat. I listened to his speech with a great deal of interest, because it gave us a great deal of information. But, as far as the political end of it is concerned, it will not be necessary for me to make any extended remarks. Whether I could derive any advantage from such a reference, if it were necessary to make it, is another question. But, I must congratulate him on the tone of his address and upon the way that he delivered it. As far as his prophecies are concerned, I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet, nor an admirer of prophecies, and therefore I will not attempt to answer that portion of his remarks, because, if we live long enough, we will all see, when the war ends, how the country will work out the problems which will confront it. I have no hesitation in expressing the belief that Canada will take care of herself.
When the war first started, I confess that the men of this country did not realize the seriousness of the situation. I believe that a great many people, especially the men. thought that the war, being over in France, or Flanders, or Russia, it did not touch us as closely as we now realize it does. Not so, however, with our women. Our women from the very first put all their energy, not only into providing comforts for our own men, their sons, brothers and fathers, but helping in Belgian Relief and Red Cross work. These women in many instances were better and more systematically organized than a great many movements, even under the Government supervision, that we have heard of.
I am not speaking now of this particular Government. The work that these women have been doing for the men at the front and for the relief of the suffering caused by this great war has been admirable and their organization has been splendid. Some of the newspapers have recently been agitating that the women should take the place of men for manual labour. Personally, I thank God that our women have not so far found it necessary to do manual labour, and I sincerely hope that it will not be found necessary in this country at any time for them to do so. During last summer as I travelled through the . country I am sorry to say I saw some farmers whose wives and daughters had to assist them in the removal of the crops, and I have no doubt that owing to the number of men who have been taken away on account of this unfortunate war, the same thing will have to be done to a certain extent in the future; but some of the news-

papers are agitating that women generally should undertake manual labour. I hope that will not be necessary. I think that for the last two or three months the people of this country have fully realized what they have to undertake. I believe that they are prepared not only to furnish the men necessary for recruiting purposes, but to pay whatever is necessary for the proper support of the army that Canada has to send to the front, no matter what the size of that army may have to be. They are ready, as the Minister of Finance has said, to economize and sacrifice to a certain extent; but they are looking to the Government for an example in the practice of economy. If the people have to economize as individuals, there is. nothing that will make them so sore, if I may use the word, as to see what they consider wastefulness on the part of this Government. Now, there may be some misunderstanding, but questions are asked US every day even with regard to the expenditure of the Militia Department. Many men ask me, on the train and off the train, at home and away from home, various questions which I will attempt to repeat. They ask me:	"Why is it necessary
for an outside	magistrate or some
such person to swear in a recruit when the officers are there to swear him in? If it is necessary, are these outside men paid for the work?" They ask me: "Why is it necessary to have an outside doctor to examine the recruits when there are doctors belonging to each battalion? If it is necessary, are these doctors paid for the work?" They ask me: "If two or three men are recruited in a village, are these men paid from the time they are recruited, from the time they are taken away from their work? Are they paid in full While they are sitting around the village shoe-shop or the village blacksmith shop doing nothing, not even drilling, or are they paid just the difference between what they would earn if they were not enlisted and what they earn as recruits?" I know that men are getting very scarce in some of the towns throughout Ontario; I do not know as to the other provinces. Is it necessary that these men, before a battalion is filled, should be left doing nothing in the villages? What benefit do we get in that way? Many people also say to me: "Is it necessary that these battalions should be kept so long drilling instead of being sent to camps with other battalions-so that they can be taught the methods of warfare as it is carried on at the front?"
1 am not complaining about these things; 1 am simply stating what people ask me and what I cannot answer. It is for the Government or for the Department of Militia to answer these questions. At the same time, the men who ask these questions are willing to support the Government to the utmost extent in recruiting; they are willing also to pay to the utmost extent to bring this country and this Empire out victorious in this war.
As I have stated, it is up to this Government to set the example in economy. In looking over the estimates for the year, one cannot help feeling that during the last four or five years, since 1911, there cannot have been such improvements made in the public service that the ordinary Estimates should have been increased from about $87,000,000 in 1911 to about $158,000,000 in 1916. Just as the manager of an institution is responsible for any increase in expenditure^ so the Government must explain the reason of this increase and tell us why the Estimates cannot be decreased without materially affecting the service that will be rendered to this country. The Government can certainly make a decrease in the Estimates of the Department of Public Works. I think .it is very bad policy for the Government of a country, just as it is for the management of a business, to put in the Estimates items that they do not intend to expend. Of course, it may be a good thing politically. I myself am a pooT politician; that is, I do not believe in taking political advantage by placing such items in the Estimates. If the Department of Public Works has no intention of erecting these buildings and constructing these various little public works, such as wharves and breakwaters, why does the Government put the items in the Estimates? It must have been for a political reason, for the purpose of convincing a section of country that benefit to them was intended by the construction of some public work at the general expense. There can be no other reason. Now, that is too bad. My hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has been telling us about the unity of this country and about doing away with politics. In the face of that it is too bad that the Government should put in their Estimates appropriations that they have no intention of spending, as acknowledged by the Minister of Finance, to the extent fo $23,000,000. There is no possible reason that I can see why the Estimates should not be cut down by $35,000,000 more, for

that amount of__ saving could be effected without injury to the public service. The Government itself should set the example if it wants the people to economize. Let us look for a moment at the expenditures that have been incurred. In the first three years of their tenure of office the Government had surpluses aggregating $133,000,-
000.	The Minister of Finance now tells us that at the end of the year the debt of this country will be $580,000,000, an increase of $243,000,000 over what it was. So that, with increased debt and expenditure of surplus, the Government have done away with $376,000,000 in something less than five years. And what have they to show for it? The Minist r of Finance may tell us of some things that they have to show, but he could not possibly make the list such as would justify this expenditure. Why, the post office expenses have jumped from about $7,000,000 or ' $8,000,000-I have not the exact figures before me-to $17,000,000 or $18,000,000. It is quite true that the Government has extended rural mail delivery, and for that I give them credit, but the expenditure on rural mail delivery would be only a drop in the 'bucket of this great increased post office expense. That increase is absolutely absurd. Now, if the Minister of Finance does noit intend to spend the $158,000,000 represented by these estimates, why cannot he strike out those amounts he does not intend to spend, as we come to them in committee? He asks us to unite with the Government in not playing politics and not talking politics. Why not, then, be honest with us and with the people and state openly what expenditures are to be made? I believe that from their estimates for public buildings and other similar works, the Government could strike out items aggregating $7,000,000 without doing a particle of harm. Then, in our expenditures on public works to be charged to oa,pital account, other great reductions could be made. They need not stop such great works as the Welland canal and the improvements at St. John and at Vancouver. Let these works go on to a limited extent. The Government need not fear that they will throw men into idleness, for the general labour market will take all the men that can be released from public works. While -I know that my friends on this side are as guilty as those on the other side in regard to the Hudson Bay railway, certainly there is no pressure this year, so far as I know, for the ex-
penditure of great sums of public money on that work.
Now I come to the revenue side of the account. The minister has shown us, and I am glad he was in a position to do so, that the revenues have increased very materially during the last six months. But I would have him remember that a great deal of that revenue has been obtained from customs charges on machinery imported for the manufacture of munitions, and that importation has about ceased. Besides, a great, deal of revenue in January and the early part of February was obtained because merchants and manufacturers throughout the country looked to see higher duties on many lines of goods. They did not know on what lines, for the minister quite properly, had not taken them into his confidence. But I know that vast -quantities of material for manufacturers were imported. Therefore, I doubt if the revenues will increase as fast during the next two months as they increased during the last two months.
The first change that 1 notice with regard to revenue is the duty on apples. My hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) said he was pleased to see that duty put on because it will help the people of British Columbia. That is one of the inconveniences of our widespread Dominion-what is meat for one province is poison for another. While this duty may benefit the people of British Columbia, it will prove a great detriment to the people of the prairie provinces. My hon. friend from North Simcoe says that no apples are shipped from Ontario or British Columbia to the Prairie Provinces. But so far as my own section of country is concerned that is not correct, for we ship many carloads of apples to the West; and, travelling in the West, I have found that there was a great consumption of Ontario apples and of British Columbia apples as well. I do not believe that we people in Ontario demanded this increased duty. For my part, I never heard it even mentioned. 1 know, from the prices that many men get who ship apples to the West, that the unfortunate people of the West must pay through the nose, as the saying is, for the apples they get. Now, while this duty may help the people of British Columbia, I would like to see them help themselves by competing with the Washington apple growers, just as people compete in any other line of business. I believe that the people of British Columbia could compete with the growers of the American West,

even without any duty, and I have no doubt the people of Ontario could hold their own against the American competition as well; -and, so far as I know, the apple-growers of Ontario are quite willing to do so.
As to the duty on crude oil, the only people upon whom this will bear very heavily, so far as I know, are the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

And the Grand Trunk
Pacific.

The Government will get something out of the Grand Trunk Pacific company by reason of the duty on crude oil, but their action is rather ungenerous, considering the amount that will be taken from the Canadian Pacific Railway company. I admit that the Canadian Pacific Railway company is a great corporation ; so far as I know they are willing to bear their share of the cost of this great war. But I think it is rather heaping it bn to take a quarter of their profits over seven per cent, at the same time hitting them on the head so far as crude oil is concerned.
In the resolution which the hon. Minister of Finance submitted in connection with his new taxation proposals I find the following :
That there shall be charged, levied and paid to His Majesty a tax of twenty-five per centum of the amount by which the profits arising from any trade or business subject to the tax in every accounting period ending after the fourth day of August, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen.
The banks, I think, end their fiscal year 'in November; therefore, their first accounting period under this legislation would begin in November, 1914. If it was my hon. friend's intention to make this legislation retroactive from the beginning of the year,
I am not sure that he will succeed; he will certainly strike those banks whose accounting periods end in the latter part of the year if he causes the tax to cover the whole accounting period. I suppose the banks have already paid the one per cent on their note issue, as provided by the Budget of last year. Some persons say you cannot strike the banks too hard. I do not agree with that. My hon. friend realizes, I am sure, that any tax imposed upon industry finally comes back to the ultimate consumer. Every large manufacturing concern knows that an increase of one-quarte.r, or one-eighth, in the charge for cheques and drafts, would compensate them for the extra taxation. In
any case, all these things come ljack to the ultimate consumer.
Clause 6 of the second resolution reads:
That the capital employed in the trade or business of an incorporated company having its head office or other principal place of business in Canada shall be the amount paid up on its capital stock.
In Ontario many companies have issued capital stock as common stock that is paid up according to the laws of the provinces. In some way they have got round the law and arranged that the stock that is issued is just as much paid up as the preferred stock. I shall not call the great companies monopolies; it is my experience that the so-called monopolies are so overloaded with overhead expenses that the ordinary small business that is well run can easily compete with it. A number of large corporations-I shall not call them monopolies- have issued a great deal of common stock and have been capitalized to such an extent that this proposed ligslation will not touch them at all. The hon. minister shakes . his head. I do not know how he is going to get out of that, because there will be lawsuit after lawsuit if he does not recognize as paid up stock the stock which the province of Ontario recognizes as such. This being the case, a number of large corporations-I need not name them-cement companies, steel companies, and other large corporations that have great quantity of common stock, will not be touched by this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There will be a definition of " amount paid up on stock " which will prevent, I think, undue advantage in the case of over-capitalization.
Undue.

That gives rise to the
observation that it is possible for a Government to take too much power into its own hands. What are we fighting for in Flanders and France? What are we spending this money for, if not to protect the right of the Englishman to be master in his own house? What are we spending this money for, if not to maintain what we call British fair play? Is it fair for the Government to take a man by the throat and make him pay what he should not pay? Is it fair for the Government arbitrarily to say what the stock of my company shall be when the Government have given me the right to issue that stock, the very Government that is going to take away that right? My hon. friend has no



right, in my judgment-leaning as I always do to British fair-play for every human being-to arbitrarily say just what that stock will be. That brings me to the people who will be most affected by the tax in the case of corporations. They are the people who are a credit to this country, those who very likely started with a small capitalization and have toiled might and day, with the greatest perseverance and industry, to work up a business in this country; and every member in this House who is in the manufacturing business and who has worked up a paying industry in this country knows what hard work it was. He knows that he kept down his capital stock and did hot try to make money out of the flotation of stock in his company, by selling it throughout the length and breadth of the land, preying on his neighbours. He has attended to his own business and made it pay and has very likely gone without dividends for ten or fifteen years to get the business in a position to compete with his neighbours in the rest of the world. He is the fallow who will have to pay one-quarter of the profits over and above his seven per cent, because he has no other recourse. Take the man who is in a partnership or who is individually carrying on business. He also has worked, as I have stated in reference to corporations-and I might call a corporation one man because in all successful corporation businesses that I know of the success largely depends on one individual in that corporation. Take the fellow who has no partners, who is doing business by himself. He has worked till he is grey headed very likely, until he has built up a business of which he is proud, and of which his town is proud-^and his country should be. He will be affected by this tax, while the great corporations, with what is sometimes called watered stock, with their great issues of capital stock, are not affected although they above all human beings in the world should be affected if you want to get at the rich man,-and I am taking it for granted that the Government want to get at the men who are capable of paying. The one person who escapes this tax is the fellow who promoted big corporations and sold the stock to everybody he could. Some of these promoters have put millions into their pockets by these promotions, yet they are not touched at all, they go scot free. I would find them if I had to take a searchlight. The man who has built up his business has to pay. I do not believe he will complain; I think he will pay and 
pay nobly without complaining. But let us be fair, that is what we are trying to do in this parliament, or should be. Bet us try and be fair to him if he is willing to pay. There is no use in driving a willing horse to death.
Now I come to the question of the $50,00b minimum. Why should it be set at $50,000?
I have been asking myself that question ever since the Budget came down. If my friend here has a company capitalised at $50,000, or is in a partnership with $50,000 invested, he is subjected to this tax; while I have only $40,000 invested, yet am making just as much in proportion as he, why should I not pay? Why should there be any limit? I do not see any sense in that. I might not have to pay as much as he, but I have just as much right to pay my proportion as the man with $50,000 invested. I do not see anv reason for arbitrarily setting $50,000, because I believe that the fellow who has not the $50,000 is just as willing to pay his proportion as the man who has, and I think he has as much right to pay as the man who has. What I do object to more than anything else is the escape of the very men, the large capitalists, who have no possible chance, in my judgment, of paying seven per cent on their capital stock. These men escape. The men who promote these corporations escape. Take the men who sit quietly on their pants and do not do a thing for the country or anybody else, the fellows who have money invested in bonds and in real estate from which they derive rents, some of them worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, why should they escape? You take that very type of man in your town; he never goes to a town meeting, never helps the town, is never willing to come forward to help with anything. He quietly gathers in his rent and his bond interest and that sort of thing. Why should he escape? I ask the minister. They are the fellows who ought to pay. Half of them are getting old and they cannot live forever and certainly they cannot take their money with them. Even when they die, in the cases of nine-tenths of them their children will quarrel like the deuce about their money. Why should such men not contribute, if only to promote peace in their families? The thing gets more absurd as we get along.
Now I come to the worst feature, the retroactive legislation. No human being can defend that. We none of us know where we are at or when we are finished.

If the Finance Minister and the Government wanted to get at the men who were supplying munitions and supplying war material for this war, why did they not take the example of a celebrated colleague now deceased and be bold enough to be honest and honest enough' to be bold, and get at them? Why whip all the other fellows over their shoulders? While I am opposed to retroactive legislation, absolutely, in any form, still, under the circumstances, considering the fact that people from one end of this country to the other say that these men who have supplied war munitions have made enormous fortunes, I believe that the people in Canada would have endorsed the action of the Minister of Militia and the Government if they had taken not one-quarter after seven per cent, but one-half.
Three-quarters.

One-half anyway of the
profits made by suppliers of munitions and various supplies to the Imperial Government and to our own Militia Department. I believe the country would have endorsed that. Why did the minister not get at these men who have made enormous profits out of the supply of munitions and not at the companies that are doing the regular business of this country? Let me give an illustration. At the end of their fiscal year the directors of a company call in their shareholders and if they have made any money, and if they are honest, they distribute it to their shareholders, who should get it, because, after all, they are the owners. Now we go back to 1914, after these corporations have distributed their profits, if they made any. Do you mean to tell me that you are going to make these men go and borrow the money to pay up the war tax from 1914? I was the other day at a meeting of an insurance company, which gave the whole of its surplus profits, $50,000, to the Patriotic Fund-a Canadian insurance company. I had the pleasure of moving the resolution. Do you mean to tell me that you are going to make that company pay as taxes $12,500 of that sum which they gave to the Patriotic Fund out of their reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was that a life insurance company?

No, it was a fire insurance company, the Gore Mutual Company, and a credit to this country. I repeat, do you mean that that company should pay as taxes $12,500 of the amount which it gave
64*
to the Patriotic Fund? So far as I can see, that would be the result of this legislation.
Now, I have an old grievance to ventilate. I want to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance the fact that he is again giving a premium to insurance companies which do business in this country without a license. He is letting companies like the New England Mutuals, Reciprocal Underwriters, and American Lloyds go scot free. I have no doubt that there are some German companies still doing business in this country, and yet the Minister of Finance practically gives them a premium for not taking out a license. I think that every company doing business in this country ought to be forced to take out a license. I do not care who they are; I would put them all on the same level, and then there would be no grumbling. But these outside companies are not taxed anything. They come to this country and do business, and are not asked to pay a cent for the benefit of this country, while the licensed companies pay for their licenses, and will be taxed under this Bill, as they were taxed under last year's Act.
I would like to speak for a moment with regard to immigration. The Estimates for immigration have not yet been passed, and perhaps I will have an opportunity of discussing the subject at greater length then. But I have a very fixed idea that if there is one branch of the Government, the Estimates for which should not have been reduced, it is the Immigration Department, because now is the time to get ready. But the Government have reduced the immigration Estimates by $1,500,000, I think, despite the fact that now is the time to prepare for the immigration that is bound to come to this country if we are not taxed too high. I hope the Minister of Finance will see to it that we are not, although it looks very doubtful in view of this Budget. We have gone all wrong in our immigration- policy. We bring immigrants here, men and women, and dump them down at the landing place, and do not look after them. We ought to make some arrangement with the provinces by which these immigrants could be taken to-suitable places and educated to a certain extent in farm work. There could be large farms in the provinces where these immigrants could get a smattering, at least, of farm work. Most of them, when they come out, are of no use for farming, and the ordinary farmer will not engage them, and educate them, and pay them at the same time. We ought to change entirely

our system of dealing with immigrants, and that is one reason why I desired to discuss this subject. But I will take the opportunity later on.
Let me say just one word with reference to what my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) spoke of so splendidly thle other evening- the patronage system. I am not here to accuse the Government of bestowing patronage in connection with the war orders;
I do not know that they did, but they say that where there is smoke there is sure to be fire, of which I got definite proof at the old Parliament buildings the other night. But I believe there is absolute corruption in connection with the system. I would certainly join with- my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and with any other member of this House who will rise and condemn the patronage system in every shape and form. Personally, I never had any patronage to dispense in the riding which I represent; I always try to treat everybody exactly the same, no matter what their politics or religion may be. Regardless of politics or religion, regardless of creed, we in this country are willing to support the Government in any reasonable expenditures required for the upkeep of the army, and in order to win victory for our arms, and for those of the Empire; but we decidedly say that these expenditures should be reduced by the Government to a minimum. I am not going to attempt to indicate the various ways in which they could be reduced-it would take me all night to do so. The Government represent the people, and they are accountable to the people. If they have not a system which enables them to know where the leakages occur they should at once organize some such system with the view of cutting off all leakages, and all patronage, because that is the curse of the whole business. The Government should .-[DOT]tart now to Teduce to the very lowest minimum the expenditures in connection with the various departments, and they can do it easily. There must be hundreds of people employed whom it is not necessary to emploj in the various departments of the Government, and there must be hunirods and thousands of items that could be reduced without any hurt to the country. I say to you, Mt. Speaker, that it is the duty of this Government to meet the wishes of the people on this point, and 1 _ bel;eve the people will be perfectly willing tu bear any reasonable expenditures neces-
sary to carry the war to a successful issue. But there will be grumbling, and certainly there should be grumbling, over the fact that in four years our ordinary expenditure has jumped from $87,000,000 to $158,000,000. Take it at the minister's own estimate, $135,000,000; why the whole thing is absurd. People would not believe it possible if they did not have it in black and white before them.
There was one point raised by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) regarding which I would like to say one word. He said that the nickel industry in Canada was controlled by Germany. I know some officers of the nickel corporation, and I know that there is not a human being in Germany who has any control, or who has anything to do with the Canadian nickel interests. I think the ministers know that as well as I do. I have been told by officers of the nickel company that they would be perfectly willing to have any investigation that might be thought desirable to clear away any doubts as to German control.	.
As it is practically six o'clock, if I started to talk further on this iniquitous, retroactive resolution that my hon. friend has introduced, I am afraid that I would have to finish after dinner; so, I will now, stop, as I have told the House frankly and plainly my views on the proposed Budget.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the wording of this section is reasonably clear. Bill No. 15, respecting the Pacific Northern and Omineca Railway Company-Mr. Green -in 'Committee.

This Bill was allowed to
stand yesterday, the point having been raised that in section 1, it was provided that the company might commence and complete the road within five years, no special time being fixed for commencement. So I have drafted the ordinary clause that is inserted in all Bills, providing that the railway may be commenced within two years and finished within five years. I move that section 1 of the Bill as it stands be struck out and this inserted in lieu thereof.
I note that in the description the expression is used, "Edmonton in the Northwest Territories". I would suggest that that should read, "Edmonton, in the province of Alberta."
I do not know that it would affect it particularly, for there is only one Edmonton.
But there is a Northwest Territories north of Edmonton.

I will be glad if the chairman will change it to read:	"Edmonton,
in the province of Alberta."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This section
covers a rather lengthy description of a great deal of which does not appear in the Bill before us. Was this description before the Railway Committee?
Yes, the section is as passed by the Railway Committee, except that it is provided that the road shall be commenced within two years and completed within five years.

Yes, "at Edmonton."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would call the attention of the committee to Rule 112, which provides that no important amendment may be proposed to any private Bill in the Committee of the Whole House unless one day's notice of the same has been given. I am subject to the direction of the committee as to whether this may be deemed an important amendment within the meaning of this rule.

I do not think the House will consider this an amendment of any importance. If any objection is taken, I am ready to move that the Bill be referred back to the Railway Committee. But the change is simply to allow the company to commence within two years and complete within five years, instead of commencing and completing within five years, as provided in the section as it stands.

On section 4-acquisition, transmission, and delivery of electric and other power:
This is the standard clause.

I do not know who drafted the standard clause, but I would point out that there is the possibility under this section that the company holding this charter might exercise its rights as an electric company without having exercised its rights as a railway company. That is to say, this charter might be used as a cover for acquiring power rights without providing a railway. There is no objection to the railway using its right of way or its authority for this purpose if it becomes established as a railway; but it is not the intention of Parliament to give the rights of a railway company to a concern that is merely for the distribution of power-at least, I take it for granted that that is not the intention of Parliament.

This is simply the standard clause inserted in these charters in this and other sessions. I do not see why. a different clause should be made for this Bill. If the

remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) apply to this Bill, they apply equally to every other similar Bill passed within the last two or three sessions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the provision of the section in question, the right of the company to acquire electric or other power or energy is limited to the purposes of its undertaking-that is, its own purposes-and it may dispose of the surplus thereof. I think that unless the company should not proceed with its undertaking, it would not have the right to acquire power or energy. However, this is a standard clause, and 1 should think it would be inexpedient just now to raise the question to which my hon. friend has referred.

I do not see why it is
inexpedient to raise the question, even though it has not hitherto been raised. Even in Parliament we live to learn; from time to time conditions are discovered that had not been observed before. This railroad has as much prospect of being built within two years as has a railroad to the moon. If it has any purpose, that purpose must be connected with the development of power. If it is the intention of Parliament to grant blanket power rights, as they do in the case of railway charters, well and good; but I do not take it that that is the intention of Parliament. Inasmuch as there is some question in the matter, I think that in all fairness that question o ught to be settled now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We might dispose of the matter by adopting the Bill in committee and dealing with the question on the third reading. The section expressly states that the power which the company may acquire shall be for the purposes of its undertaking and subject to the provisions of section 247 of the Railway Act. No good reason appears to have been given why this company should be singled out for exceptional treatment. In view of the fact that this is a standard clause, and that section 247 of the Railway Act makes provision relative to a company of this kind which may acquire power and use the surplus, it would seem to me that the committee would be safe in adopting this section. Then, if-my hon. friend desires to raise the question on the third reading, it might be more conveniently dealt with at that stage.

I should be very glad to
accept the view of the Minister of Finance, but if the details of any private Bill are to

be considered, they should be considered either in the standing committee or in the Committee of the Whole. As the point was not raised in the standing committee, here and now is the place to have it raised and settled. I did not hear the route of the railway laid down, but I am under the impression that the route approximates certain valuable water powers. There is a possibility that we may grant to this company fights and powers in regard to these water powers, while the company is professing merely to desire a railroad charter, and Parliament is professing to give them no more than that. If they build a railway let them have the benefit of the standard clause; but I certainly wish to have it provided that they shall not get the benefit of the water power clause unless the railroad is built.

This Bill is simply a renewal of a charter already granted. The company may not use this power unless it appertains to their undertaking. This particular section was inserted not by the promoters of the Bill, but by the Railway Committee. I do not see why this company should be singled out for special treatment so far as the standard clause is concerned. I would suggest that the Bill pass through committee in the ordinary manner, and if there is any reason fpr objecting to this particular clause in the Bill, the matter might be taken up when the Bill comes up for third reading.

This is the time and place to raise any point such as I have raised. Of course, if the majority of the House think that the point is not well taken, I shall not delay the committee, but in my humble judgment the question is a very important one, and is very pertinent to this particular charter, whatever may have been the case with regard to other charters. I should like to have the matter settled now.

If I have caught the
apprehension of the hon. member for Edmonton, it is that the company might, while masquerading as a railway company, be in existence only for the purpose of developing and selling power; that it might, in a word, undertake to develop power without building a railway at all. The hon. gentleman suggests that the company might argue that though the railway was not built, the power was being developed for the purposes of the railway when it should be built. I would not like'to undertake to give a judicial decision as to the possibility of this taking place under section 40. The com-

pany might, of course, even though its undertaking were not actually in operation, be developing power for the purposes of that undertaking, and might argue that it had the right to sell that power under those conditions. I draw the attention of the hon. member for Edmonton to the latter phrases of the section, by which the company is forbidden to sell any power, except with the consent of the Railway Commission. Supervision is reserved to that commission, which must fix the rates. I understand that clause was framed by that commission itself. The commission would have power, should they come to the conclusion that the company, while pretending to be developing power for the purposes of its undertaking was not yeit in esse and was really selling power, to refuse to that company the right to sell at all. It would have power to refuse that company the right to sell at all. We have therefore the protection of the first phrase, which says, "for the purposes of the company." Then we have the protection of Section 247 of the Railway Act. And further we have the protection of the Railway Commission. Consequently I do not think we could improve matters much by referring the section back.

Mr J. E. ARMSTRONG {East Lambton): Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest and pleasure to many of the speeches that have been delivered in the course of this debate, and I must congratulate the members who have taken part on the reasonable criticisms which they have offered. We have heard a great many splendid patriotic utterances this session, and I am sure we all appreciated the speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir-George Foster) the other evening. I would even go a step further' than the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and say that bitter partisan politics will not be displayed on the floor of this Parliament for many years to come; nor do I think they will be exhibited to any great extent in the country districts, There were two memorable speeches to which I would like to refer. I congratulate the right hon. the leader of the Opposition on the splendid tribute he paid to the late Sir Charles Tupper, and also upon the speech he delivered on ihe extension of the life of Parliament. I am sure that these speeches will be read with a great deal of interest and pleasure in years to come. We also feel deeply grateful, especially those on this side of the House, for the splendid effort of the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White), when he placed before this House and the country this excellent Budget. While it is open to reasonable criticism, we must recognize the fact that Canada is at war, that she is fighting for her very existence, and that the people must expect exceptional war measures will be introduced from time to time until the close of the war and that extraordinary taxes must be collected in order that we may carry to a successful conclusion our share of the struggle. I am sure that after all is said and done we can do nothing less than congratulate the Minister of Finance and the Government upon placing before Parliament such a splendid measure for demanding a reasonable share of the profits of the great manufacturers and financial institutions of the country. Never let it be said again that the Government are tied
R-i

up to the great financial, railway, and manufacturing interests. Never in the history of the country has a Finance Minister attempted to gather from the financial institutions of Canada a reasonable and fair portion of the immense wealth which they are taking from the people. While it is true that some of our prominent men say that this is radical legislation, that it is bordering on socialism, yet, in talking with a number of prominent manufacturers and business men since the Budget was introduced, I have been assured by them that they are willing to assist in providing the means for carrying on the war and that they will gladly pay the portion that is demanded of them by the Minister of Finance.
It has also been said that this is a Budget in favor of the agricultural interests and the workingmen. Well may it be so said. The workingmen and the farmers are left free as far as this new taxation is concerned. On the other hand, one of the great departments of agricultural industry has been assisted by an added duty. x
We have listened to-day to the address of the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and I hope he will not expect me to deal with many of the matters which he brought forward. He urges that economy be observed by every department of the Government and I am sure that the members on both sides of the House earnestly hope and Believe that the Government will exert their best efforts to promote economy in every branch of the service. He calls attention to the Estimates. The hon. gentleman knows full well that the items in the present Estimates that were left over from last year are revotes. The Government have already explained that they .do not intend to go on with the public works to which these items apply until such time as they have sufficient funds to continue them. Should the war cease before the end of the year, and should they have sufficient money to carry on these public works, hon. gentlemen opposite will not complain about carrying on works which they were willing enough to pass at the last session.
We also found the hon. member for North Oxford making the statement that the duty on apples would be meat for British Columbia and poison for the West and that the Ontario fruit growers had not asked for a duty on apples. A similar statement was made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. 
A. K. Maclean) in his speech on the Bu,dget. He said:
In my judgment in no province of Canada outside of British Columbia are the apple growers interested in this increased duty.
Let me call the attention of these hon. gentlemen to the fact that on the seventh day of last month the fruit growers of Ontario met in the city of Toronto and passed a unanimous resolution whereby they appointed delegates to go to Ottawa and urge upon the Finance Minister the need of an increased duty on apples. In face of that we find hon. gentlemen opposite saying that the fruit men of Ontario did not ask for this, did not need it and did not want it. These gentlemen came to Ottawa, and I had the pleasure of introducing them to the Finance Minister; so I feel that I know what I am talking about when I make the statement that the fruit growers of Ontario are deeply interested in this question and are very anxious that this duty should be placed on apples. It will be recalled that five years ago 1,400 fruit men from Ontario 9 p.m. met in the old chamber of the House of Commons and urged an increase of duty on the then Government. Hon. gentlemen opposite must appreciate the fact that as far as the Ontario fruit growers are concerned they are vitally interested in this question. You must also take into consideration the fact that the fruit-growing industry is one of the greatest that we have in Canada according to Mr. C. C. Moore, the market expert of the Department of Agriculture, who states that $127,000,000 is invested in that industry. Of that suip the following amounts are invested in apple orchards in the different provinces:
Ontario	$50,000,000
British Columbia	 20,000,000
Nova Scotia	 20,000,000
Quebec		10,000,000
This is therefore an enormous industry and one worthy of the consideration of this House.	,
Let us look at a few more facts in connection with this industry. For many years past both the old Government and this Government have been sending out literature to foreign lands urging people to come and paitake of the good things we have in store for them in the fruit districts of this country. Tens of thousands of people have come to our shores and spent millions of dollars in the development of the fruit industry, in the hope and belief that they would be able to make use

of the markets of this country. I believe that the people of the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, are willing to live and let live as far as this industry is concerned, and that they realise the importance of the Vast development which 'has taken place in the fruit industry in British Columbia since 1891. At that time there was only a very small acreage, while to-day 2,500,000 acres of fruit lands are under development in that province. The Department of the Interior are issuing literature showing the great advantages of that province in fruit production. When you remember the enormous acreage that has been planted in apples in the northwestern States, you can readily understand the position in which the fruit men of British Columbia find themselves. The states of Idaho, Washington and Montana have.planted so enormously that the estimate has gone forth that they are producing to-day eleven or twelve times as much fruit as they can dispose of in their own- country to advantage; 500,000 acres of apple orchards have been planted in those northwestern states, largely for the purpose of disposing of their product in our western provinces. Canada, with her splendid opportunities for the production of fruit and the enormous acreage that she has capable of development, you cannot but agree with me that the time has now come when we should to a reasonable extent look after this great fruit industry. The Government of British Columbia has sent earnest petitions to this Government urging it to place this dirty upon apples, and different organizations in that province have also sent delegations to place before this Government the strongest representations in support of an increased duty on fruit. Therefore, in face of the fact that according to the census of 1911, we have in the Dominion of Canada 14,800,000 apple trees, and only 60 per cent of them bearing, it is well for us to consider whether we should allow the great states in the northwest to dump into the western provinces an inferior quality of fruit, as they have been doing during the last few years. I have been urged to state to the House that the fruit growers' associations of the provinces of British Columbia and of Ontario believe that they will be able to deliver fruit in the western provinces at a price not exceeding the price now being paid by the people living there. The people of the western provinces, the Grain Growers' Association and the United Farmers of Alberta, should take into consideration the fact that the fruit trusts of the United States have control of the sale of fruit in the different towns and cities of their provinces. If they investigate, they will find that such is the case; and in future, if this additional duty is imposed, and if the Grain Growers' Association and the United Farmers of Alberta will get in touch with the fruit growers' associations in the provinces of British Columbia and Ontario, they will find that these associations will gladly meet them and ship to them at a small profit the enor-ipous quantities of fruit which they require, and I hope that they will take advantage of the offer of these associations.
Canada is one of the largest apple producing countries in the world; she exports to-day apples to the extent of 1,200,000 barrels per annum. Now, some hon. gentlemen from the eastern provinces have said that the fruit growers of Nova Scotia do not need this added protection. For instance, the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) said that the proposed increase would not be of any value to the province of Nova Scotia. I cannot but believe that when the hon. gentleman made that statement he was not closely m touch with the apple producers of that province. Although this province is a large exporter of apples and its market is the export trade market, its apple growers must expect that, unless some protection is given in the western provinces the fruit production of Ontario will interfere materially with their export trade. Only-sixty per cent of the enormous area bearing, and we cannot tell what the production will be when all the orchards that are already planted come into bearing.
The hon. junior member for Halifax also made the following statement:
I do not believe that the imposition of this duty will he of any advantage to the apple industry of British Columbia.
I do not need to argue that point; I think hon. members on both sides will readily understand that the imposition of this duty will be of untold benefit to the apple producers of British Columbia.
Let me give just one instance in which an increase in the duty on fruit has not increased the cost to the consumer. In 1874 the men who were interested in the grape industry of this country came to Parliament urging that the duty on grapes be increased. The Government of that day increased the duty by ten per cent, but the

grape growers found that it was impossible for them, with that small duty, to develop the industry, and so they came back, and in 187^9 the Government raised the duty to two cents per pound. What was the result?,' The grape growers of this country planted out extensive vineyards, and within a few years the people of Canada were able To buy grapes at a lower price than the duty charged on them. What do we find,to-day? In the Niagara district, in the fall of the year, grapes can be purchased at one and a half cents per pound, and that condition of things has existed for manj\ years past.
The hon. junior member for Halifax gave us to understand that the increased duty on oil would nqt be of benefit to the farmers of the West. So far as gas and fuel oil is concerned, the farmers of the West do not use it in any quantities worth speaking of. Gas and fuel oil is used largely on the railways through the wooded areas of this country. The Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and several other railways are using gas and fuel oil extensively. While I have no intention of criticising the placing of an import duty on this article, I wohld suggest to the Minister of Finance that, after the war is over, he will probably fihd that the munition plants, which are using enormous quantities of this gas and fuel oil at present, will not require it in large quantities. I hope that when, that time conies he will.give to the railways the use of this oil for motive power and the advantage qf importing it free. My reason for this suggestion will be explained,by a reference to the report of the Commission of Conservation. On page 44 of that,report I find this statement:
Locomotive Fuel.
Oil fuel is in exclusive use on 477 miles of the Canadian Pacific railway, on 134 miles of the Esquimau and Nanaimo railway, and on 115 miles of the Great Northern railway, a total of 726 miles, all in British Columbia. In no case has a definite report been submitted of a fire caused by an oil-burning engine in Canada. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway has announced that during the spring and early summer of 1915, oil-burning engines will be installed on that portion of its lines in British Columbia and Alberta between Prince Rupert and Jasper, a distance of 71S miles. It is expected that this action will materially decrease the danger of fire along this portion of the line. The use of oil fuel is purely voluntary with the railways, and its adoption is dictated altogether by business considerations.
Anything that we can do towards conserving our great natural resources, our timber

resources as well as others, should be done, and quickly done. When we consider the enormous fire waste constantly going on in those timber areas traversed by railways the benefit to the people of any steps to prevent forest fires is at once apparent, Hon. members who have travelled over the new Transcontinental, lines must have seen the wilful waste of our great forest wealth under the conditions which have been allowed to exist in the building of our great roads. Tens of thousands of acres of timber and pulpwood lands have been burned over, and not for generations, can that forest cover be restored. I offer my suggestion not in a faultfinding way to the Minister of Finance. I do not say that the great corporations seriously complain about this duty, but I do say that it is worthy of the minister's consideration whether this duty should not cease with the end of the war, providing the production of crude oil in Canada does not increase! Unless we can encourage the use of this fuel, or can compel the railways to use electric power on their lines through our forest areas, we may expect that the enormous losses of the past will be repeated by the further destruction of our forests. One other statement was made in this debate, and this is practically the last to which I shall refer-the statement made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) in the quotation of a long communication from a farmers' organization in his district. The hon. gentleman said that there were 800 of those men, and that one of them had stated that the price of gasolene had increased from thirty to fifty per cent. Knowing the hon. member from Medicine Hat to be a fair-minded man, I was somewhat surprised that he did not take into consideration the fact that gasolene was free of duty except for the duty of 7J per cent imposed last session. This would amount to only a little over one cent a gallon. That being the case, the hon. gentleman should not have presented to the House a statement that would lead the people to believe that this Government was responsible for great increase in the price of gasolene. I do not believe that he so intended it, and I cannot help thinking that he will tqll the people of his section of the country that they were mistaken in this regard. They could have brought in tank cars or tank wagons, and so could have obtained the gasolene at the price in the market of production, plus the duty of about one cent a gallon.

As a number of questions have been asked in the House, and as I have been asked personally many questions on the subject, I feel that I should put on record a few facts, in order that honourable gentlemen may understand more about this product. Gasolene of Canadian quality still comes in free of duty, except for the 7\ per cent war tax imposed last session. The gasolene largely used in the United States is not allowed in, owing to its heavier quality. Canadian gasolene costs two cents a gallon more to manufacture, and is much better. The gasolene used in many districts in the United States is five points below the Canadian product, being 59 beaume, as against 64 required by the Canadian regulations. Regard must be had also to the difference in the size of the gallon. In the United States they use wine measure, while in Canada we use imperial measure, which is about one-fifth larger. Allowing for the size of the gallon and the quality of the oil, even with the war tax, the price of gasolene is not higher in the principal centres of Canada than at corresponding points in the United States.
The price of gasolene to-day in Detroit per wine gallon from the tank wagon is 18 cents, or equal to 21 cents per Imperial gallon. Under item 272 of the tariff, gasolene under -725 specific gravity at 60 degrees temperature is admitted into Canada free. The gasolene offered for sale from the tank wagons in Detroit would not qualify for admission free into Canada, since it is 59 beaume, or -7407 specific gravity. It is an altogether heavier gasolene, costs about 2 cents per gallon less to manufacture and can be purchased at 2 cents less in the market. Crude oil in the United States, from which so much of the Canadian gasolene is made, costs to-day two and three times as much as jt did nine months ago. For instance, in the mid-continent fields it sold for 40 cents a barrel a year ago, and to-day is selling from $1.30 to $2 per barrel, or from Si to 5 times as much as it did then. The war in Mexico for the past two years, together with the shutting off of the production in Roumania, Central Europe, and Russia, appears to have left the world dependent on the United States supply. These causes, together with the enormous increase in the uses to which gasolene is put, particularly the tractors and motors, have all contributed to the [DOT]rise in .price, which has not been peculiar to Canada but has been generally worldwide. The demand for gasolene is now and will probably be during 1916, greater
than the available supply, as the production of naphtha-bearing crude oils has not kept pace with the constantly increasing consumption. The large increase in (the number of automobiles, motor boats, farm tractors and stationary gas engines has brought the gasolene price to its present level. The following figures will show why the price of gasolene has increased so enormously. In 1905 there were approximately 1,200 automobiles registered in the Dominion of Canada. In 1910, 10,000 cars were in operation and in 1915, 83,000. The automobile manufacturers estimate that in 1916, there will be over 3,000,000 cars in operation in Canada and the United States. In 1905 probably not one gasolene tractor was owned in the Dominion of Canada. In 1910, 2,000 of these machines were in operation, and in 1915, there were' approximately 8,000 gasolene tractors in the Dominion. The average high power gasolene tractor consumes a barrel of gasolene every ten working hours. In 1905 it is estimated that only 5,000 stationary gas engines were * in use in the Dominion. By 1910 this number had increased to 25,000, and at the present time there are over 100,000 of these machines, all helping to swell the figures for gasolene consumption. In 1905 Canada used approximately 100,000 barrels of gasolene, and in 1910, approximately 390,000 barrels. In 1915 the consumption of gasolene in the Dominion was over 1,300,000 barrels. Most of the gasolene refined in Canada is manufactured from United States crude oil, as the production of crude oil in the Ontario field is not large. Unfortunately the great increase in the number of gasolene consuming machines has not been followed by a proportionate increase in the production of crude oil; in fact some of the large naphtha producing crude oil fields in the United States have shown a marked falling off in production. The great Cushing field in Oklahoma is now producing considerably less than 100,000 barrels per day, as against 300,000 barrels per day which it was producing a year ago. My hope is that some inventive genius will evolve a practical kerosene carburetor which would enable a large proportion of the motor driven vehicles to operate with refined oil as fuel. Refined oil is a drug on the market. The price of gasolene has increased by leaps and bounds. For instance, in the city of Toronto for the past seven months, tank wagon prices per Imperial gallon were as follows:- August 1, 134c.; September 1, 16c.; October 1, 17c.; November 1, 184c.; December 1, 22c. ;

January 1, 24c.; February 1, 25c. The same prices pervailed in other large cities near the International boundary line.
I , am very glad ito have the privilege of referring these matters, which are of interest to the district that I represent. We all appreciate the significance of the fact that this country is in the throes of a great war. The northern half of this continent is ours-ours to maintain and to develop. If the national ideals of Germany should ever hold sway in this country, we should lose the privileges and liberties that are our common heritage. It is hardly necessary to say that we decline to accept the national ideals of Germany, of Austria, or of Turkey. The happiness or misery of eight millions of people, the control and development of hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of productive industry and capital in this country, are at stake. Hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House-indeed, the whole of the people of Canada-are desirous of taking such steps as may bring this war to a successful conclusion. Never was Canada more united in a common cause; never was she more determined to do her part to attain a worthy end. Our brave soldiers on the battlefields of France and Belgium are singing:
*We'll never let the old flag fall;
We love it the best of all.
We don't want to fight To show our might,
But when we do, we fight, fight, fight!
Our gallant boys are ready and willing and able to fight for the land they love so well and for the flag they hold so dear. When we realize that Great Britain has trebled her national debt and doubled her taxes, the amount being asked by the Finance Minister to-day seems but small. We should be glad and proud that we have controlling the affairs of Canada men who are able to guide its destinies in the manner in which they are being guided. We all love our country; we believe in her; we live for her; we are ready to fight for her, in order that her territory may remain intact and her name untarnished.
Mr. DUNCAN C. BOSS (West Middlesex):	Mr. Speaker, as this is the first
opportunity that I have had of addressing the House this session, I trust that you will not think it presumptuous on my part if I tender to you my congratulations upon your elevation to the high office which you occupy. Although my congratulations are late, they are none the less sincere. You pos-

sess all the qualities necessary to your office. The university of your native province has marked you as being possessed of scholarly attainments. We on this side of the House feel that, in addition to that, you are so inspired by ideals of fairness, justice and honour that you will be able to hold the scales in equal poise between the parties, unmoved by fear, favour or affection.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the various addresses of those who have taken part in this debate. I have listened .to none with more interest than to the lion, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). It is always a pleasure to listen to him; we esteem him one of the first orators of Canada. We know his wide experience in public life, and we know his intense patriotism and love for his country. His speech of a few days ago was only another instance of that eloquence, another manifestation of that patriotism. As I listened to him my mind travelled back over the space of several years, and I thought of a speech which I heard him make in 1910 when I had newly come to this Parliament. I think that, without exception, it was the most eloquent speech I ever heard. He then dwelt on the necessity of Canadians being able to fight for themselves, on the prowess of Canada, on its future potentialities and on all its coming greatness. I sat and listened to him in open admiration, as did every member on this side of the House. The other night he spoke to us about the evils of politics in this country and the evils of the patronage system, and I concurred also in all he had to say. My fear is only this, that the hon. minister may do as he did in 1910 when, a few moons having passed, the minister took a double back somersault in the air. I fear that now he will not, in the council chamber, inspire in the Prime Minister the same views that he expressed in this House on the evils of patronage and will not, as a member of the Privy Council of Canada, endeavour to do away with what he describes as this monster of iniquity, the patronage system. I hope he may, because I think patronage is one of the great evils of this country.
I wish first to discuss a few things that affect this country in relation to the war. Many of these matters have already been touched upon in a very able manner by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). Some things which he said should be accentuated, and in my humble way I am going to associate myself with him in urging these matters. In the first place, I think if we are going to carry on this war to a success-

ful issue, as we certainly are, and if we are going to get 500,000 soldiers to fight for King and country, we must make sure that these soldiers are going to the battlefield with perfectly contented minds and that they feel satisfied that the dear ones they are leaving behind will be protected just as if they were remaining at home. They must feel sure that if they are injured on the field of battle they will be taken care of and if they lose their lives the dear one they leave behind, wives, mothers and children, will receive generous protection from the people of this country. It seems to me we cannot be too careful about this matter and that, although our allowances are generous to the woman and children left behind, they are not placed upon a proper basis. I was struck by a remark of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) ivho spoke of a man fighting in the trenches, under his command, a noble, brave soldier, one worthy of the Victoria Cross, a man who had left a wife and twelve children behind him. I could not get a better instance to typify or symbolize what 1 wanted to say. Here is a married man in the field, fighting the battles of liberty in Canada, with twelve children at home, and this country gives that wife the paltry allowance of $20 a month for her sustenance and that of her family. I think in this regard we are derelict in our duty. The British system is far better and I cannot understand why the principle we have adopted in regard to our pensions is not followed in Tegard to our separation allowances. Whether a roan is dead or alive, his children will require as much to support them. If a man dies on the battlefield his widow has certain allowances, and she gets a certain allowance for each child. Why should not that system be followed also in regard to our separation allowances? For my own part I think the same principle should apply, and that some change should be adopted by this Government in that respect. I would like to emphasize the point made by the hon. member for Edmonton, that the pensions given to the rank and file of our soldiers, particularly those in the lower ranks, are insufficient. A single man who _ has been totally disabled in the face of the enemy receives from this country $22 a month, and he is also entitled to an allowance of $7.33 a month for an attendant. It strikes my judgment that this is not sufficient to give to a man who has risked his life for liberty and for this country, and comes
back here totally incapacitated from earning a living for himself. I would commend to the favourable consideration of the Government a pamphlet issued by a committee of which Mr. Frank Darling is chairman, and I should wish to associate myself with the suggestions in that pamphlet, because they are all worthy of commendation.
We are engaged in the most terrible war that any land has ever been engaged in; the fury and fanaticism and strife and turmoil and noise of battle in this war are such as have never occurred before. Men are not only losing their lives and their limbs, but, what is even more pathetic and sad, men are losing their reason; men are having their nervous systems shattered; quite a few of them have come back to this country with those sweet' bells of the mind jangled out of tune; and it seems to me that some special*provision should be made for them. Up to the present I believe no special provision has been made. These men should not be put in the ordinary insane asylum, but special institutions should be built for them where they will receive unusual consideration, as there is no real life for them in the future.
The treatment of our officers is not very liberal, and should be improved. I was not aware until recently that they are treated less liberally than the British officers; 1 thought they received a little more; but the fact that they are paid less only accentuates the argument I wish to make. As I understand our present system, an officer who joins the active forces to-day is allowed by the Government $150 for uniform and accoutrements. As I understand the English system, a similar allowance is made to the British officer, but while our Canadian officer receives only one allowance for this purpose, no matter how long the war lasts, the British officer receives an allowance when he first goes on service, and each year thereafter receives about £20 for uniform and accoutrements. That is only just treatment of our officers. Their clothes cannot last for ever; in the struggle and strife of active army life their uniforms must wear out and become soiled, and I think it only fair that these officers who are risking their lives should receive an allowance of say $100 a year to replenish their uniform and accoutrements.
I shall not follow seriatim what the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) has been saying. My hon. friend is my nearest neighbour, and we have ever been friends. He has been a constant visitor to West Middlesex for many years. He

always conies probably when we least need him; but if his visits have been as pleasant to him as they have been innocuous to me, I do not mind how often he cornes. Some day in the future I may do myself the honour of returning some of them, and I hope that my visits to his constituency will have better results than he secured.
My ibon. friend discussed the question of apples. He made some remarks in regard to apples which I could not follow. The part of the country from which I come is a part in which many apples are grown, the best apples in the world, I venture to say, not excluding those grown in the county of Lambton. I cannot understand the solicitude of the hon. member for East Lambton for the apple industry of this country. I could not follow his argument. He said, forsooth, that the apple growers of this country had 14,000,000 trees, that it was a great industry, and that the apple growers had sent petitions and delegations to the Government asking to have their industry protected. I cannot see that that is any reason for giving them additional protection. I cannot understand why the hon. member should have got so much worked up over this small industry.
